malrules.name: Add-Numerators-Add-Denominators
malrules.description: When adding fractions with different denominators, students incorrectly add numerators together and denominators together, treating the operation as component-wise addition. For example: 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5 (incorrect). This error reflects a fundamental misunderstanding where students treat fractions as two independent whole numbers rather than a single quantity representing a ratio. Research shows this stems from 'whole number bias' - the overgeneralization of whole-number arithmetic properties to fractions (Ni & Zhou, 2005; Behr et al., 1984).

malrules.name: Common-Denominator-Numerator
malrules.description: Students add numerators and add denominators when adding fractions, believing that adding denominators creates a 'common denominator.' This is a variant of the whole number bias error (Ni & Zhou, 2005) where students show partial procedural knowledge (awareness that common denominators are needed) but lack conceptual understanding of how to find them. For example: 1/4 + 1/6 = 2/10 = 1/5 (incorrect; correct answer is 5/12).

malrules.name: Denominator-Comparison-Error
malrules.description: Students incorrectly compare fractions by focusing on the denominator value, believing that a larger denominator means a larger fraction. For example: 1/4 > 1/3 because 4 > 3 (incorrect). This error reflects 'whole number bias' (Ni & Zhou, 2005) - the overgeneralization of whole-number comparison rules where larger numbers always mean 'more.' Students fail to understand the inverse relationship: larger denominators mean smaller pieces.

malrules.name: Ignore-Denominators
malrules.description: Students operate only on numerators, completely ignoring denominators, treating fraction operations as whole-number arithmetic on the 'top numbers' only. For example: 2/3 + 1/5 = 3 (just adds 2+1). This error reflects a fundamental failure to understand that a fraction is a single number with magnitude, not two separate numbers. Research shows this stems from students processing 'numerator and denominator as two separate whole numbers' (Pitkethly & Hunting, 1996; Nunes & Bryant, 1996).

malrules.name: Keep-Common-Denominator-For-Multiplication
malrules.description: Students incorrectly keep the common denominator when multiplying fractions with like denominators: (a/b)×(c/b) = (a×c)/b instead of (a×c)/(b×b). For example, (2/5)×(3/5) = 6/5 instead of the correct answer 6/25. This is an overgeneralization error where students apply the fraction addition rule (keep the common denominator) to multiplication. Newton et al. (2014) found students were particularly prone to this error on like-denominator problems.

malrules.name: Multiply-Across-For-Division (Failure to Invert)
malrules.description: Student treats fraction division like multiplication, forgetting to invert (flip) the second fraction before multiplying. This error reflects a failure to apply the 'invert and multiply' algorithm correctly. For example, (2/3)÷(4/5) = (2×4)/(3×5) = 8/15 instead of the correct (2/3)×(5/4) = 10/12 = 5/6. Research shows this is a widespread difficulty for students as well as pre-service and in-service teachers (Ma, 1999; Tirosh, 2000).

malrules.name: Natural-Number-Bias-Numerator-Only (Whole Number Bias)
malrules.description: Students incorrectly compare fractions by comparing their numerators only, ignoring the denominators entirely. They believe that a larger numerator means a larger fraction. For example: 3/4 < 5/8 because 3 < 5 (incorrect). This is a manifestation of the 'natural number bias' or 'whole number bias'—the tendency to apply natural number properties inappropriately to rational numbers.

malrules.name: Subtract-Across (Independent Whole Number Error)
malrules.description: When subtracting fractions with different denominators, students incorrectly subtract the numerators AND subtract the denominators: a/b - c/d = (a-c)/(b-d). For example: 3/4 - 1/2 = (3-1)/(4-2) = 2/2 = 1 (incorrect; correct answer is 1/4). Brown & Quinn (2006) documented this error in their analysis of algebra students' fraction errors, finding that students 'demonstrated the error of adding or subtracting numerators and denominators across' by extending whole number operations to fractions.
